thinkers.name: Jensen Huang
thinkers.bio: Co-founder and CEO of NVIDIA, whose GPUs and CUDA software stack became the dominant hardware platform for training and running deep learning models after 2012. He has been the leading public advocate of 'accelerated computing', 'AI factories' and 'sovereign AI'.

influence: Framed the industry's infrastructure narrative (accelerated computing, AI factories, sovereign AI) adopted by governments and hyperscalers.
foresight: Early, sustained bet on GPUs for AI and correct calls on compute demand after DeepSeek; some calls (AGI-by-tests, $3-4T) unresolved.
allocation: Controls the scarcest input of the AI boom; allocation of GPU supply shapes which labs and countries can scale.
contribution: CUDA, DGX systems and data-center GPUs are the core commercial substrate of modern AI.
corpus: Many keynotes, earnings calls and interviews, but heavily promotional and rarely falsifiable.
future: Roadmap (Blackwell, Rubin) and China/export policy positions directly shape 2026-2030 compute supply.

mentalModel.summary: After AlexNet showed GPUs could train deep nets, Huang repositioned NVIDIA around deep learning; in 2016 he hand-delivered the first DGX-1 to OpenAI. GPUs were framed as the engine of a new AI computing model.
Argued that AI would 'eat software' and that the end of CPU scaling made accelerated (GPU) computing the successor architecture; deep learning was still concentrated in a few internet companies.
Framed generative AI as a platform shift and data centers as factories producing intelligence; demand for accelerated computing reached a 'tipping point'.

Pushed 'sovereign AI' (every nation should own its AI infrastructure), claimed the ~$1T installed data-center base would shift to accelerated computing within a few years, gave a conditional five-year AGI-by-tests forecast, and said AI would make programming unnecessary for most people.

Treated reasoning/inference scaling as a multiplier on compute demand (100x for reasoning models) and dismissed DeepSeek-driven fears; called export controls a failure that accelerated Chinese rivals; forecast $3-4T AI infrastructure spend by 2030 and cited $500B Blackwell+Rubin visibility through 2026.
Raised Blackwell+Rubin expectations to ~$1T through 2027 and argued China's market would open 'over time', while Nvidia guided to zero China data-center compute revenue.

reversals.from: 'China is going to win the AI race' (FT summit)
reversals.to: 'China is nanoseconds behind America in AI' — America must race ahead and win developers
reversals.trigger: Immediate backlash to the FT remark in Washington; same-day clarification on X.

reversals.from: Useful quantum computers 15-30 years away (CES, Jan 2025)
reversals.to: Publicly said he had been wrong; hosted Quantum Day at GTC
reversals.trigger: Market reaction and pushback from quantum-computing firms.

thinkers.name: Satya Nadella
thinkers.bio: CEO of Microsoft since 2014; made the 2019 bet on OpenAI that put GPT models on Azure and into Microsoft products (Bing, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365 Copilot).

influence: Shaped the enterprise framing of AI (copilots, agents, Jevons paradox, GDP as the AGI test).
foresight: Early on conversational interfaces and OpenAI; overestimated Bing's search disruption and early Copilot uptake.
allocation: Directs one of the largest AI capex budgets and was OpenAI's main financier.
contribution: Commercialized frontier models at enterprise scale via Azure and Copilot.
corpus: Earnings calls, long-form podcasts (Dwarkesh, BG2), essays and keynotes.
future: Azure capacity, OpenAI stake (~27%) and Copilot distribution make Microsoft pivotal through 2030.

mentalModel.summary: Saw 'conversation as a platform': bots as the new apps and human language as the new UI, alongside a human-AI partnership ethic (2016 Slate essay).
Bet that large-scale models trained on Azure supercomputers would be a platform shift, investing $1B in OpenAI (2019) as its exclusive cloud.
Moved fast to productize GPT-4: AI-powered Bing to challenge Google ('made them dance'), copilots across Office, and backed Altman during the Nov 2023 OpenAI crisis.
Hedged OpenAI dependence by hiring Suleyman to build Microsoft AI; argued agents would collapse SaaS business logic into an 'AI tier'.

Argued efficiency gains (DeepSeek) would raise total demand (Jevons paradox); dismissed self-declared AGI milestones in favor of GDP growth as the real test; renegotiated the OpenAI deal; identified power, not chips, as the binding constraint.
Azure passed $100B annual revenue and Copilot reached ~30M paid seats while capex kept rising.

reversals.from: Exclusive compute provider to OpenAI with AGI determination left to OpenAI's board (2019-2023 structure)
reversals.to: Non-exclusive relationship, AGI claims verified by an independent expert panel, Microsoft free to pursue AGI on its own
reversals.trigger: OpenAI's compute needs and restructuring into a PBC; Nadella's stated skepticism of self-declared AGI milestones.

thinkers.name: Sundar Pichai
thinkers.bio: CEO of Google since 2015 and Alphabet since 2019; declared Google 'AI-first' in 2016 and oversaw Google Brain/DeepMind, the Gemini models, TPUs and the integration of generative AI into Search.

influence: Agenda-setting slogans (AI-first, 'more profound than fire') more than technical ideas.
foresight: AI-first call was early; 'low-hanging fruit is gone' underestimated 2025 progress; AGI timing unresolved.
allocation: Controls one of the largest AI capex budgets plus TPUs, DeepMind and Search distribution.
contribution: Google invented the transformer and built Gemini/TPUs, though productization lagged OpenAI in 2022-23.
corpus: Founders' letters, earnings calls and some long interviews; mostly measured corporate language.
future: Owns a full stack (chips, cloud, models, Search, Android, YouTube) that shapes AI distribution.

mentalModel.summary: Declared a shift from mobile-first to AI-first; the computer would become an intelligent assistant (2016).
Called AI more profound than electricity or fire while stressing its risks must be managed.
After ChatGPT, moved from cautious release of LaMDA to launching Bard and AI in Search (Feb 2023) and merging Brain with DeepMind.
Argued under-investing in AI was a bigger risk than over-investing; reported that over a quarter of new Google code was AI-generated; predicted progress would get harder in 2025.
Described current systems as 'AJI' and placed AGI a bit after 2030; warned of 'elements of irrationality' in the boom and that no company would be immune to a correction.
Kept raising capex (2026 guidance roughly double 2025) while Gemini gained share against Microsoft's Copilot.

reversals.from: Cautious, 'responsible' slow release of conversational models (LaMDA withheld 2021-22)
reversals.to: Rapid public launch of Bard and generative AI in Search
reversals.trigger: ChatGPT's launch (Nov 2022) and Microsoft's Bing+OpenAI challenge.

thinkers.corpusNotes: Pichai rarely makes dated, falsifiable forecasts; claims are mostly framing and capex justifications. Alphabet 2026 outcomes were not verifiable by search this session (search budget exhausted).

thinkers.name: Mark Zuckerberg
thinkers.bio: Founder and CEO of Meta; created FAIR (2013), championed open-weight Llama models (2023-24), pivoted capital from the metaverse to AI, and in 2025 launched Meta Superintelligence Labs.

influence: Made open-weight frontier models a mainstream strategy (Llama) and popularized 'personal superintelligence'.
foresight: Metaverse bet and 'Llama will be most advanced by 2025' did not pan out; energy-constraint call was early and correct.
allocation: Sole control of Meta's ~$100B+/yr capex and talent spending.
contribution: FAIR, PyTorch and Llama shaped the open AI ecosystem.
corpus: Earnings calls, letters and podcasts, but evidence this session is recalled, not re-verified.
future: Massive capex and distribution to 3B+ users, but uncertain model leadership.

mentalModel.summary: Saw AI research as core to Facebook's future and created FAIR under Yann LeCun (2013).
Strongly optimistic about near-term AI benefits; called AI doomsday talk irresponsible.
Bet the company's next platform on the metaverse, renaming Facebook to Meta (Oct 2021) and forecasting a billion metaverse users within a decade.
Declared a 'year of efficiency' and pivoted priority to generative AI, releasing LLaMA and open-licensed Llama 2.
Set a goal of building general intelligence and open-sourcing it responsibly; argued open source would become the industry standard like Linux and that energy, not chips, would bound scaling.

After Llama 4 disappointed, reorganized around Meta Superintelligence Labs, invested in Scale AI, declared superintelligence 'in sight', and signaled more selective open-sourcing; argued the risk of under-spending exceeded misspending hundreds of billions.
Capex guidance rose to roughly $115-135B while metaverse budgets were trimmed (recalled, not re-verified).

reversals.from: Metaverse as Meta's primary next platform and investment priority
reversals.to: AI as the top priority (metaverse folded into AI-enabled wearables)
reversals.trigger: 2022 stock collapse, ChatGPT, and investor pressure ('year of efficiency').

reversals.from: Open source AI is the path forward; Llama to be released openly as the industry standard
reversals.to: Need to be careful about what Meta chooses to open source; frontier work centralized in a superintelligence lab
reversals.trigger: Llama 4's weak reception, Chinese open models overtaking Llama, and safety/competitive concerns about superintelligence-level models.

thinkers.name: Liang Wenfeng
thinkers.bio: Co-founder of quant fund High-Flyer and founder of DeepSeek, whose open-weight V3 and R1 models (Dec 2024 - Jan 2025) showed near-frontier performance at much lower reported training cost and shook AI markets.

influence: DeepSeek R1 reset assumptions about cost, open weights and China's position.
foresight: Early compute stockpile and the claim that closed-source moats are temporary were borne out (provisional).
allocation: Self-funded lab via High-Flyer; limited by export controls.
contribution: MLA/MoE efficiency, GRPO-based RL reasoning and MIT-licensed releases.
corpus: Only a handful of interviews (2023, 2024); very few public statements.
future: Central to China's open-model ecosystem and domestic-chip adoption.

mentalModel.summary: Used High-Flyer's quant profits to build GPU clusters (Fire-Flyer), accumulating ~10,000 A100s before US export controls, betting that compute would be strategic.
Founded DeepSeek (2023) explicitly to pursue AGI through fundamental research rather than near-term applications or outside financing.

Held that closed-source moats are temporary, that team and culture are the real moat, that China must become an original innovator rather than a follower, and that chip embargoes, not money, were the binding constraint; priced DeepSeek-V2 near cost.
Released R1 openly (MIT license); became a nationally recognized figure, attending symposia with Premier Li Qiang and Xi Jinping; made almost no public statements thereafter.

reversals.from: Applying machine learning to quantitative trading at High-Flyer
reversals.to: Building a dedicated AGI research lab (DeepSeek)
reversals.trigger: ChatGPT/LLM breakthrough and existing GPU cluster capacity.

assertions.claim: Software is eating the world, but AI is going to eat software.
assumptions: Deep learning generalizes beyond internet companies to enterprise software
Learned models can replace hand-written code for many functions
assertions.predictedOutcome: AI-generated or AI-driven functionality progressively displaces conventional hand-coded software across industries.
assertions.contextAtTime: In 2017 deep learning was used at scale mainly by a few internet companies; transformers had just been proposed; few enterprises used ML in production.
assertions.outcome: By 2026 AI coding agents and LLM features were pervasive, and fears that AI agents would displace per-seat SaaS triggered a large software-stock selloff in early 2026, though incumbent software revenues kept growing.
assertions.verdictRationale: The directional claim, made when AI was marginal in enterprise software, has largely materialized: AI is reshaping how software is built and priced. It was metaphorical rather than precisely testable, so credit is directional.
assertions.evolution: Repeated through 2026 in the same form; no revision found.

assertions.claim: Accelerated computing and generative AI hit a tipping point; the ~$1 trillion installed base of data centers will in a few years be all accelerated computing, as data centers become 'AI factories'.
assumptions: Generative AI demand persists beyond a hype cycle
CPU performance scaling stays slow
Customers can monetize AI to justify spend
assertions.predictedOutcome: Data-center spending shifts decisively from general-purpose CPUs to GPU/accelerated systems over the following few years, with sustained surging demand for NVIDIA.
assertions.contextAtTime: NVIDIA data-center revenue had just jumped after ChatGPT; many analysts expected a digestion phase or double-ordering correction in 2024-25.
assertions.outcome: Demand kept surging: NVIDIA data-center revenue reached $89.0B in the quarter ended July 2026 (+117% y/y), and hyperscaler capex rose sharply into 2026. CPU servers still exist, so the literal 'all accelerated' has not happened.
assertions.verdictRationale: The demand-surge and AI-factory build-out components proved right through mid-2026, against widespread expectations of a correction; the literal claim that the whole installed base becomes accelerated is not yet testable or met.
assertions.evolution: Scaled up in 2025 to a $3-4T AI infrastructure forecast by 2030 (see as-huang-8).

assertions.claim: Every country needs to own its own AI infrastructure ('sovereign AI'), because AI codifies a nation's culture, intelligence and history; leaders should build the infrastructure as fast as they can.
assumptions: Governments see AI as strategic national infrastructure
Nations will spend public money on domestic compute rather than rely on US hyperscalers
assertions.predictedOutcome: Governments and state-linked entities become a major new class of AI-infrastructure buyers.
assertions.contextAtTime: Sovereign compute was a niche idea in early 2024; most AI compute was bought by US hyperscalers and labs.
assertions.outcome: Through 2025-26 numerous national and Gulf state AI build-outs and 'AI clouds' emerged (recalled; e.g. Saudi, UAE, European initiatives), and NVIDIA's 'AI clouds/industrial/enterprise' customers accounted for a large share of data-center revenue in 2026. Independent quantification of sovereign spend not verified this session.
assertions.verdictRationale: The sovereign-AI category clearly materialized as a buyer segment, but its scale relative to hyperscalers could not be independently verified this session; also partly a sales pitch.
assertions.evolution: Became a standing theme in NVIDIA keynotes through 2026; no revision found.

assertions.claim: If AGI is defined as passing every human test you can imagine, AI will do well on every one within five years; under other definitions AGI may be much further away.
assumptions: Benchmark/test performance continues to scale with compute and data
Test-passing is an adequate operationalization
assertions.predictedOutcome: By ~2029 frontier AI passes essentially all human professional and academic exams, including specialized medical boards.
assertions.contextAtTime: GPT-4 passed the bar exam but struggled with some specialized medical exams; reasoning models did not yet exist.
assertions.outcome: By 2025-26 reasoning models reached gold-medal level on the IMO and high scores on many professional exams, but harder benchmarks remained unsaturated; the horizon has not passed.
assertions.verdictRationale: Deadline (2029) not reached; progress is on track for the narrow test-passing definition he explicitly conditioned on.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: It is the job of computing technology to make it so nobody has to program; the programming language is human, so children should focus on domain expertise rather than learning to code.
assumptions: LLMs become reliable enough to translate natural language into working software
Domain expertise becomes the scarce skill
assertions.predictedOutcome: Natural-language programming becomes mainstream and reduces the need for most people to learn conventional programming.
assertions.contextAtTime: GitHub Copilot autocompletion was common, but autonomous coding agents were not yet usable; most experts still advised learning to code.
assertions.outcome: By 2025-26 natural-language 'vibe coding' and coding agents were mainstream (e.g. over a quarter of new Google code AI-generated by late 2024; agent tools triggering a 2026 SaaS selloff), but professional programming did not disappear.
assertions.verdictRationale: Direction (natural language as the programming interface) proved right faster than most expected; the stronger implication that people need not learn programming is not established.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: Reasoning models can consume 100 times more compute, and future reasoning models will consume much more compute; DeepSeek R1 is an excellent innovation that increases, not decreases, demand.
assumptions: Test-time compute scaling keeps improving model quality
Cheaper reasoning expands usage faster than per-query efficiency falls
assertions.predictedOutcome: Despite efficiency gains like DeepSeek's, aggregate demand for NVIDIA compute keeps rising strongly.
assertions.contextAtTime: DeepSeek's low reported training costs had just triggered a ~17% one-day NVIDIA selloff and fears of a compute glut.
assertions.outcome: NVIDIA revenue more than doubled year over year to $96.2B in the quarter ended July 2026, with data-center revenue up 117%; hyperscalers raised capex sharply.
assertions.verdictRationale: Made against the prevailing market fear, the claim that reasoning and efficiency would expand compute demand was borne out by 2026 demand data. Interested party, but the outcome is independent.
assertions.evolution: Reinforced at GTC 2025/2026; no revision found.

assertions.claim: US export controls on AI chips to China were a failure: they cut NVIDIA's China share from ~95% to ~50% and motivated and accelerated Chinese competitors; later, 'China is going to win the AI race' (walked back to 'nanoseconds behind').
assumptions: Chinese domestic chips (e.g. Huawei Ascend) can substitute adequately
Beijing will favor domestic suppliers when US chips are restricted
assertions.predictedOutcome: Continued controls would cost NVIDIA the Chinese market and strengthen Chinese chip and AI ecosystems rather than slow them.
assertions.contextAtTime: H20 sales had just been restricted ($5.5B charge); DeepSeek had shown Chinese labs could compete on constrained hardware. Anthropic and others argued for tighter controls.
assertions.outcome: By 2026 NVIDIA's China data-center sales were near zero: even after the US licensed H200 sales, Beijing withheld approval to foster domestic suppliers, sales were under 1% of data-center revenue, and NVIDIA guided to no China data-center revenue.
assertions.verdictRationale: His prediction that NVIDIA would lose China and that China would push domestic substitutes was borne out; whether controls 'failed' at slowing Chinese AI, and whether China 'wins', remain contested and unresolved.
assertions.evolution: Shifted from '95% to 50%' (May 2025) to '95% to zero' (Oct 2025) to 'China will win' then 'nanoseconds behind' (Nov 2025), and in May 2026 'the market will open over time'.

assertions.claim: AI infrastructure spending will reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by the end of the decade.
assumptions: AI revenues grow enough to justify capex
Power and supply-chain constraints are overcome
No sharp financing pullback
assertions.predictedOutcome: Annual AI infrastructure spend of roughly $3-4T by ~2030.
assertions.contextAtTime: Huang cited ~$600B in 2025 hyperscaler data-center capex; bubble concerns were widespread.
assertions.outcome: Spending kept climbing into 2026 (e.g. Microsoft quarterly capex ~$41B, Alphabet and Meta guiding roughly to doubled 2026 capex), but the 2030 target is years away.
assertions.verdictRationale: Deadline not reached; 2026 capex is on an upward trajectory consistent with but far from proving the forecast.
assertions.evolution: Reiterated after the Nov 2025 earnings; no revision found.

assertions.claim: NVIDIA has roughly $500 billion of Blackwell and Rubin demand visibility through calendar 2026 (raised at GTC 2026 to ~$1 trillion through 2027); there is no AI bubble.
assumptions: Customer commitments convert to shipments
Financing for AI labs and neoclouds holds up
assertions.predictedOutcome: Blackwell+Rubin revenue of ~$500B over 2025-2026.
assertions.horizon: through calendar 2026 (and 2027 for the raised figure)
assertions.contextAtTime: Analysts questioned the figure (part already shipped; trued-up backlog ~$307B); AI-bubble talk peaked in late 2025.
assertions.outcome: By the quarter ended July 2026 NVIDIA was reporting $96.2B quarterly revenue and guiding $108B for the next quarter, consistent with the trajectory; calendar 2026 is not complete.
assertions.verdictRationale: The window (end-2026) has not closed; run-rate through mid-2026 is consistent with the claim, but the total cannot yet be checked.
assertions.evolution: Raised to ~$1T through 2027 at GTC 2026.

assertions.claim: Bots are the new apps; human language is the new UI ('conversation as a platform').
assumptions: NLP becomes good enough for open-ended conversation
Users prefer conversational interfaces to apps for many tasks
assertions.predictedOutcome: Conversational agents replace a large share of app interactions.
assertions.contextAtTime: Pre-transformer NLP; the 2016 chatbot wave (Messenger bots, Cortana, Microsoft's Tay failing the same week) was brittle.
assertions.outcome: The 2016 bot wave fizzled, but LLM-based chat (ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini) made conversation a mass-market interface from 2023, with agents spreading in 2025-26.
assertions.verdictRationale: The thesis was right but the 2016 technology could not deliver it; it came true only after LLMs, roughly seven years later.
assertions.evolution: Revived in 2023 as 'copilots' and in 2024-25 as agents (see as-nadella-5).

assertions.claim: Invest $1B in OpenAI and become its exclusive cloud, jointly building Azure AI supercomputers aimed at AGI (followed by ~$10B in 2023).
assumptions: Scaling large models on massive compute will produce commercially valuable capabilities
Exclusive cloud access confers platform advantage
assertions.predictedOutcome: OpenAI models become a major driver of Azure and Microsoft product revenue.
assertions.contextAtTime: GPT-2 had just been released; scaling laws were not yet published; most of big tech did not back an outside lab at this scale.
assertions.outcome: Microsoft's stake in OpenAI Group PBC was valued at ~$135B (~27%) in Oct 2025, OpenAI committed an incremental $250B to Azure, and Azure passed $100B annual revenue in FY2026.
assertions.verdictRationale: A contrarian bet made before scaling laws were established, it generated large strategic and financial returns by 2025-26.
assertions.evolution: Hedged in 2024 (Suleyman's Microsoft AI) and restructured in Oct 2025 (non-exclusive compute, expert-panel AGI test).

assertions.claim: With the AI-powered Bing, Microsoft would challenge Google, 'the 800-pound gorilla' in search: 'I want people to know that we made them dance.'
assumptions: Chat-based answers erode Google's search advantage
Early access to GPT-4 confers a lasting product lead
assertions.predictedOutcome: Bing gains meaningful search/AI-assistant share from Google.
assertions.contextAtTime: ChatGPT had reached ~100M users; Google appeared caught flat-footed and Bard's demo had a factual error.
assertions.outcome: Google did respond (Bard, AI Overviews, Gemini), but by 2026 Gemini was outpacing Microsoft's consumer Copilot and Google's search franchise remained dominant.
assertions.verdictRationale: The literal claim (forcing Google to react) came true, but the implied market-share shift in search did not occur.
assertions.evolution: No public revision found; Microsoft's consumer focus shifted to Copilot under Suleyman.

assertions.claim: Copilots will be the new UI for knowledge work; Microsoft 365 Copilot priced at $30 per user per month for enterprises.
assumptions: Enterprises see enough productivity ROI to pay a large per-seat premium
Model quality sufficient for everyday Office tasks
assertions.predictedOutcome: Rapid, broad paid adoption of Microsoft 365 Copilot across the commercial seat base.
assertions.contextAtTime: Generative AI enthusiasm was peaking; ROI evidence for enterprise copilots did not yet exist.
assertions.outcome: Microsoft 365 Copilot reached ~30M paid seats by mid-2026 (per a low-reliability report), a small fraction of Microsoft's several-hundred-million commercial Office seats, after a slow 2024 ramp.
assertions.verdictRationale: Adoption became material by 2026 but far slower and narrower than the 'every knowledge worker' framing implied.
assertions.evolution: Messaging shifted in 2024-25 from copilots to agents.

assertions.claim: Business applications are essentially CRUD databases with business logic; in the agent era that logic will migrate to AI agents and SaaS business apps as we know them will collapse.
assumptions: Agents become reliable enough to operate across systems of record
Value shifts to an 'AI tier' above databases
assertions.predictedOutcome: Per-seat SaaS business apps lose value to agent layers; vendors restructure around agents.
assertions.contextAtTime: Agents were early and unreliable; SaaS revenues were growing normally.
assertions.outcome: In Feb-Mar 2026 software stocks sold off sharply on exactly this fear (SEG SaaS Index -25.7% YTD at March 31), though software earnings were still growing and some recovery followed.
assertions.verdictRationale: Markets priced the thesis in 2026, but no actual collapse of SaaS revenues had occurred by October 2026; open-ended.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: Jevons paradox strikes again: as AI gets more efficient and accessible, its use will skyrocket, turning it into a commodity we just can't get enough of.
assumptions: Demand for AI is highly price-elastic
Efficiency gains (e.g. DeepSeek) lower prices rather than just margins
assertions.predictedOutcome: Cheaper AI increases total compute and cloud demand rather than shrinking it.
assertions.contextAtTime: DeepSeek R1 had just triggered fears that cheaper models would shrink demand for GPUs and data centers.
assertions.outcome: Azure grew ~40%+ into 2026 and passed $100B annual revenue; NVIDIA data-center revenue more than doubled y/y; hyperscaler capex rose.
assertions.verdictRationale: Made in the middle of a market panic, the claim that efficiency would expand demand was borne out by 2026 usage and capex data.
assertions.evolution: Microsoft briefly slowed some data-center leases in early 2025, then resumed heavy capex; no revision of the view found.

assertions.claim: Self-claiming some AGI milestone is nonsensical benchmark hacking; the real benchmark is whether the world economy grows at ~10% (developed world ~7%).
assumptions: Transformative AI would show up in productivity and GDP statistics
assertions.predictedOutcome: AGI should not be declared until macro growth visibly accelerates.
assertions.contextAtTime: OpenAI's contract with Microsoft let OpenAI's board declare AGI, which would cut off Microsoft's IP rights; labs were touting benchmark wins.
assertions.outcome: No acceleration of global growth toward 10% was evident by 2026; in Oct 2025 the renegotiated deal required any AGI declaration to be verified by an independent expert panel.
assertions.verdictRationale: This is a criterion rather than a forecast; it was reflected in the 2025 contract, but whether AI eventually drives such growth is unresolved.
assertions.evolution: Became part of the Oct 2025 contract (expert-panel AGI verification).

assertions.claim: The binding constraint on AI build-out is no longer chip supply but power and ready data-center shells; otherwise chips end up 'sitting in inventory that I can't plug in'.
assumptions: Grid interconnection and construction lag GPU supply
assertions.predictedOutcome: Power availability, not GPUs, limits hyperscaler AI capacity growth in 2026.
assertions.contextAtTime: GPU supply had loosened relative to 2023-24; utilities and grid queues were becoming the bottleneck; Zuckerberg had made a similar argument in 2024.
assertions.outcome: Microsoft kept capex at record levels into 2026 (~$41B in the June 2026 quarter); no independent 2026 source on power-limited deployments was gathered this session.
assertions.verdictRationale: Plausible and widely echoed, but not independently verified with 2026 outcome data in this session.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: Over time, the computer itself, whatever its form factor, will be an intelligent assistant helping you through your day; we will move from mobile first to an AI first world.
assumptions: Machine learning keeps improving across speech, vision and language
Assistants become the primary interface
assertions.predictedOutcome: AI assistants become a primary computing interface and Google reorients around AI.
assertions.contextAtTime: Weeks after AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol; voice assistants were narrow; transformers did not yet exist.
assertions.outcome: By 2025-26 general AI assistants (Gemini, ChatGPT, Copilot) were mass-market, and Gemini was gaining against Copilot; Google's whole stack had reoriented around AI.
assertions.verdictRationale: An early, clear strategic forecast that materialized, though Google was not first to deliver the breakthrough assistant (OpenAI was).
assertions.evolution: Reaffirmed repeatedly; no revision found.

assertions.claim: AI is one of the most important things humanity is working on; more profound than, I dunno, electricity or fire — but like fire, its downsides must be overcome.
assumptions: AI becomes a general-purpose technology with economy-wide effects
assertions.predictedOutcome: AI's long-run impact exceeds that of electricity.
assertions.contextAtTime: Before transformers were widely used; AI mainly in recommendation, search and perception.
assertions.outcome: AI became the dominant technology investment theme of 2023-26, but its civilizational significance relative to electricity is not yet assessable.
assertions.verdictRationale: Not falsifiable on a 2026 horizon.
assertions.evolution: Repeated on 60 Minutes in 2023; no revision found.

assertions.claim: Launch Bard and bring generative AI into Google Search, ending Google's cautious slow-release posture.
assumptions: Search's moat survives the shift to AI answers if Google integrates them itself
Google's models can catch up to OpenAI
assertions.predictedOutcome: Google defends search leadership by integrating generative AI rather than being displaced by chatbots.
assertions.contextAtTime: ChatGPT's success and Microsoft's Bing launch led many to predict the decline of Google search; Google reportedly declared a 'code red'.
assertions.outcome: Google shipped AI Overviews (2024), AI Mode and Gemini; by 2026 Gemini was outpacing Microsoft's Copilot and Google remained the dominant search provider, while publishers reported traffic losses.
assertions.verdictRationale: The defensive integration strategy succeeded in preserving Google's position through 2026, though it came after OpenAI had seized first-mover advantage.
assertions.evolution: Accelerated with Gemini (Dec 2023) and AI Overviews (May 2024).

assertions.claim: The risk of underinvesting is dramatically greater than the risk of overinvesting in AI infrastructure; even if over-invested, the infrastructure is widely useful to Google.
assumptions: AI is a platform shift where losing position is costlier than excess capacity
Excess capacity can be redeployed internally
assertions.predictedOutcome: Alphabet keeps raising AI capex despite ROI questions.
assertions.contextAtTime: Analysts were beginning to question AI capex returns (e.g. Sequoia's '$600B question', summer 2024).
assertions.outcome: Alphabet capex rose to ~$91B in 2025 and was guided to roughly $175-185B for 2026 (recalled); Pichai himself warned of 'elements of irrationality' in Nov 2025. Whether the spend earns adequate returns is not yet known.
assertions.verdictRationale: A risk judgement whose payoff depends on long-run AI returns that cannot yet be measured.
assertions.evolution: Paired in Nov 2025 with an acknowledgment of bubble-like irrationality (see as-pichai-7).

assertions.claim: I think the progress is going to get harder. When I look at 2025, the low-hanging fruit is gone; the hill is steeper (though there is no definitive wall).
assumptions: Pretraining scaling returns are diminishing
New breakthroughs needed for further gains
assertions.predictedOutcome: Visible AI capability gains in 2025 slow relative to 2023-24.
assertions.contextAtTime: Reports that OpenAI's next model showed smaller gains; Altman said 'there is no wall'; o1-style reasoning had just appeared.
assertions.outcome: Pretraining-only gains did slow, but 2025 brought large capability jumps via reasoning/RL and test-time compute (e.g. IMO gold-level results, Gemini 2.5 and Gemini 3) and surging compute demand.
assertions.verdictRationale: Right that easy pretraining gains were exhausted, but wrong if read as a slowdown in overall 2025 progress, which accelerated via new techniques, including at Google.
assertions.evolution: By mid-2025 he described current systems as 'AJI' with rapid progress expected through 2030.

assertions.claim: We are in an era of 'artificial jagged intelligence' (AJI); AI will make dramatic progress by 2030 but full AGI will likely arrive somewhat after 2030.
assumptions: Uneven capabilities persist and require further breakthroughs to fix
assertions.predictedOutcome: No broadly accepted AGI before ~2030; large capability advances before then.
assertions.contextAtTime: Peers (Altman, Amodei) were giving 2026-2028 timelines; Hassabis said 5-10 years.
assertions.outcome: No consensus AGI by October 2026.
assertions.verdictRationale: Horizon not reached.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: The AI investment boom is both rational and has elements of irrationality; if the bubble bursts, no company is going to be immune, including Google.
assumptions: Investment is outpacing near-term revenue
A correction would propagate across the ecosystem
assertions.predictedOutcome: A possible correction in AI investment that would hit all players, while long-run impact remains profound.
assertions.contextAtTime: Late-2025 bubble debate after circular deals among OpenAI, NVIDIA, Oracle and AMD.
assertions.outcome: Through Oct 2026 no broad AI investment collapse occurred; capex and NVIDIA revenue kept rising, while AI-exposed software stocks did see a sharp 2026 selloff.
assertions.verdictRationale: A conditional warning whose condition (a burst) had not occurred by the cutoff.
assertions.evolution: Coexists with his 2024 'underinvesting is the bigger risk' stance.

assertions.claim: Create a dedicated fundamental AI research lab (FAIR) led by Yann LeCun.
assumptions: Deep learning will be core to Facebook's products
Open research attracts top talent
assertions.predictedOutcome: Facebook becomes a leading AI research organization.
assertions.contextAtTime: One year after AlexNet; Google had acquired DNNresearch (Hinton); deep learning was not yet mainstream in industry.
assertions.outcome: FAIR produced PyTorch and the Llama models, but its influence waned after 2025 reorganization into Meta Superintelligence Labs and LeCun's departure in Nov 2025.
assertions.verdictRationale: An early bet on deep learning that produced foundational tools (PyTorch) and the Llama line.
assertions.evolution: FAIR deprioritized relative to MSL in 2025.

assertions.claim: Within the next decade, the metaverse will reach a billion people, host hundreds of billions of dollars of digital commerce and support jobs for millions of creators and developers.
assumptions: VR/AR hardware becomes mass-market
Social presence in 3D drives engagement
assertions.predictedOutcome: ~1B metaverse users by ~2031.
assertions.contextAtTime: Pandemic-era enthusiasm for virtual worlds; generative AI was not yet mainstream.
assertions.outcome: Reality Labs accumulated >$70B in operating losses; metaverse budgets were reportedly cut by up to ~30% in late 2025 as resources moved to AI and AI glasses (recalled).
assertions.verdictRationale: Deadline (2031) not reached, though the trend through 2026 is strongly against the forecast.
assertions.evolution: De-emphasized from 2023 in favor of AI (see reversal).

assertions.claim: Meta's long-term vision is to build general intelligence and open source it responsibly; Meta will have ~350,000 H100s (~600,000 H100-equivalents) by end of 2024.
assumptions: Scaling compute yields general intelligence
Open release is compatible with safety and Meta's business
assertions.predictedOutcome: Meta becomes a frontier lab releasing open models toward AGI.
assertions.contextAtTime: Llama 2 was the leading open model; Meta had pivoted from the metaverse a year earlier.
assertions.outcome: Meta built the compute, but its open frontier strategy faltered after Llama 4 (2025); it reorganized under Meta Superintelligence Labs and signaled more selective open-sourcing.
assertions.verdictRationale: An aspiration; AGI not reached and the open-source component was partly abandoned.
assertions.evolution: Recast in 2025 as 'personal superintelligence' with selective open-sourcing.

assertions.claim: Energy, not chips, will become the binding constraint on scaling AI: gigawatt-scale data centers take years of permitting and power build-out.
assumptions: Demand for training/inference compute keeps growing exponentially
Grid expansion is slow and regulated
assertions.predictedOutcome: Power availability becomes the main bottleneck for AI data centers within a few years.
assertions.contextAtTime: In early 2024 GPU supply was still the widely cited bottleneck.
assertions.outcome: By late 2025 Microsoft's CEO said its constraint was power and data-center shells rather than chips, and gigawatt-scale campuses became the norm.
assertions.verdictRationale: He identified power as the next bottleneck when chips were the consensus constraint; an independent peer confirmed it by late 2025. Outcome evidence is a single interested party, so confidence is moderate.
assertions.evolution: Meta later announced gigawatt-scale campuses (Prometheus, Hyperion) consistent with this view (recalled).

assertions.claim: Open source AI is the path forward: like Linux, open models will become the industry standard, and starting next year Meta expects future Llama models to become the most advanced in the industry.
assumptions: Open ecosystems out-iterate closed labs
Meta can sustain frontier training and still release weights
assertions.predictedOutcome: Llama models lead the industry from 2025 and open models become the standard.
assertions.contextAtTime: Llama 3.1 405B had just closed much of the gap with GPT-4o; DeepSeek and Qwen were rising but less visible in the West.
assertions.outcome: Llama 4 (April 2025) did not lead and drew criticism; the strongest open-weight models of 2025 came from Chinese labs; Meta formed MSL and signaled it would be careful about open-sourcing frontier models. Open weights did spread (even OpenAI released gpt-oss).
assertions.verdictRationale: The specific, dated forecast that Llama would be the most advanced in 2025 failed; the broader open-weights trend was partly right but led by others.
assertions.evolution: Walked back in the July 2025 'Personal Superintelligence' letter (selective open-sourcing).

assertions.claim: In 2025, Meta and other companies will have an AI that can effectively be a sort of mid-level engineer writing code.
assumptions: Coding agents become reliable on real codebases within a year
assertions.predictedOutcome: During 2025 AI agents do substantial mid-level engineering work at Meta.
assertions.contextAtTime: Coding assistants were strong at autocomplete; autonomous agents (Devin etc.) were unreliable.
assertions.outcome: Coding agents improved dramatically in 2025 and drove a 2026 SaaS selloff, but no public evidence was found that Meta's agents functioned as mid-level engineers in 2025.
assertions.verdictRationale: Capability trend was right in direction, but the specific claim of mid-level-engineer equivalence in 2025 was not demonstrated.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: Form Meta Superintelligence Labs, invest ~$14.3B in Scale AI and hire top researchers at extreme pay because developing superintelligence is now in sight; aim for 'personal superintelligence' while being careful about what to open source.
assumptions: Superintelligence is achievable within a few years with sufficient talent and compute
Talent concentration can close Meta's frontier gap
assertions.predictedOutcome: Meta returns to the frontier with superintelligence-class models within a few years.
assertions.contextAtTime: Llama 4 had disappointed; OpenAI, Google and Anthropic led; peers gave 2026-2030 AGI timelines.
assertions.outcome: Meta continued heavy spending (2026 capex guided ~$115-135B, recalled); LeCun left in Nov 2025. Status of MSL frontier models by Oct 2026 could not be verified this session.
assertions.verdictRationale: Outcome of the superintelligence push is not yet assessable.
assertions.evolution: Marks a reversal from the 2024 open-source stance.

assertions.claim: If Meta ends up misspending a couple of hundred billion dollars that would be unfortunate, but the risk is higher on the other side: being out of position if superintelligence arrives sooner.
assumptions: The payoff from leading in superintelligence dwarfs capex losses
Meta's ad cash flows can absorb overspending
assertions.predictedOutcome: Meta keeps escalating capex despite bubble risk.
assertions.contextAtTime: Late-2025 AI bubble debate; Meta raising capex and taking on off-balance-sheet data-center financing.
assertions.outcome: Meta guided 2026 capex to roughly $115-135B (recalled); returns not yet assessable.
assertions.verdictRationale: A risk judgment whose outcome depends on future AI returns.
assertions.evolution: Consistent with Pichai's 2024 underinvestment argument; no revision found.

assertions.claim: High-Flyer acquired ~10,000 Nvidia A100 GPUs (by 2021) for its Fire-Flyer clusters before US export controls, a compute base later used for DeepSeek.
assumptions: Large-scale compute would be strategically valuable and scarce
assertions.predictedOutcome: Owning a large GPU cluster becomes a decisive advantage for Chinese AI work.
assertions.contextAtTime: In 2021 few Chinese firms outside big tech bought GPUs at this scale; export controls on A100s came in Oct 2022.
assertions.outcome: US controls (Oct 2022 onward) cut off A100/H100-class sales; DeepSeek used its stockpile and H800s to train V3/R1, becoming China's leading open model lab.
assertions.verdictRationale: The pre-control stockpile proved strategically decisive; however the action was made for quant trading, so the 'belief' about LLMs is partly retrospective.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: DeepSeek will pursue AGI through fundamental research rather than near-term applications or commercialization, without seeking outside financing.
assumptions: High-Flyer profits can fund frontier research
A small, young, research-driven team can compete with big tech
assertions.predictedOutcome: DeepSeek becomes a research-first frontier lab rather than an application company.
assertions.contextAtTime: Chinese 'hundred-model war' after ChatGPT; most startups raised VC and chased applications.
assertions.outcome: DeepSeek released V2, V3 and R1 as research-led open models with novel efficiency techniques and remained largely focused on models rather than consumer monetization; AGI not achieved.
assertions.verdictRationale: The organizational aspiration was carried out, but its stated goal (AGI) is unresolved.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: In the face of disruptive technologies, moats created by closed source are temporary; even OpenAI's closed-source approach cannot prevent others from catching up. A team's culture and talent are the real moat.
assumptions: Algorithmic efficiency and open publication diffuse capabilities quickly
Compute gaps can be partly offset by efficiency
assertions.predictedOutcome: Open models (including DeepSeek's) catch up to closed frontier models, eroding closed-source advantages.
assertions.contextAtTime: OpenAI's GPT-4o led; Llama 3 was the leading open model; DeepSeek was known mainly for cheap V2 pricing.
assertions.outcome: DeepSeek-V3 (reported ~$5.6M final training run) and R1 (MIT license) approached o1-level reasoning, triggering a ~17% NVIDIA one-day drop; OpenAI later released open-weight gpt-oss models and its Microsoft deal was revised to allow open weights.
assertions.verdictRationale: Within six months DeepSeek itself demonstrated that closed leads were narrow, and closed labs moved toward open weights; frontier leadership nonetheless stayed with closed US labs.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: China's AI cannot remain a follower; Chinese firms must contribute original innovation rather than free-ride. Money is not DeepSeek's problem; the embargo on high-end chips is.
assumptions: Chinese researchers can produce frontier-level original work
Compute restrictions are the binding constraint
assertions.predictedOutcome: Chinese labs move from imitation to original contributions while chip access limits scale.
assertions.contextAtTime: Western consensus held that Chinese labs lagged 1-2 years and mostly followed US innovations.
assertions.outcome: DeepSeek's MLA/MoE efficiency methods and GRPO-based reasoning were widely adopted; Chinese labs led open-weight models in 2025. Huang called China 'nanoseconds behind'. Chip constraints persisted: NVIDIA's China sales stayed near zero in 2026 amid US and Chinese restrictions.
assertions.verdictRationale: Chinese original innovation and the chip bottleneck were both borne out, though overall frontier leadership remained with US labs.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

assertions.claim: Price DeepSeek-V2's API near cost (far below rivals), reflecting architecture-driven cost reductions rather than a deliberate price war.
assumptions: MoE + latent-attention efficiency sharply lowers serving cost
Cheap access grows the user/developer base
assertions.predictedOutcome: Inference prices collapse and efficiency becomes a competitive axis.
assertions.contextAtTime: Chinese LLM APIs were priced near Western levels; efficiency was not the main competitive narrative.
assertions.outcome: Major Chinese providers (ByteDance, Alibaba, Baidu) cut prices within weeks (recalled), and DeepSeek's efficiency later reset global expectations about training and inference costs.
assertions.verdictRationale: The pricing move precipitated a price war and showcased efficiency gains that reshaped the market in 2025.
assertions.evolution: No revision found.

relations.note: Huang said he disagreed with almost everything Amodei says, rejecting his warnings of mass entry-level white-collar job loss and the idea that only a few should build AI.

Amodei argued (Jan 2025) for strong US chip export controls on China; Huang called export controls a failure that strengthened Chinese competitors. Positions documented separately; no direct exchange cited here.
Huang called DeepSeek R1 an excellent innovation and praised its open-sourcing, while arguing it increases compute demand.
Both argued that DeepSeek-style efficiency gains would expand rather than shrink AI compute demand (Nadella's 'Jevons paradox' post; Huang's '100x compute' for reasoning).
$1B investment and exclusive Azure partnership (2019), followed by multi-billion investments; ~27% stake valued ~$135B in Oct 2025.
Backed Altman during the Nov 2023 OpenAI board crisis, offering to hire him and Brockman, then welcomed the board changes.
Nadella dismissed self-declared AGI milestones as 'benchmark hacking', implicitly pushing back on AGI claims tied to the OpenAI contract; Altman not named.
Nadella said the OpenAI-powered Bing would make Google 'dance'; Pichai later replied that one shouldn't play to someone else's dance music.
Nadella hired Suleyman to lead the new Microsoft AI organization, building in-house models to reduce dependence on OpenAI.
Pichai's 'AJI' (artificial jagged intelligence) framing was reported as crediting Karpathy's 'jagged intelligence' term.
Zuckerberg called AI doomsday warnings 'pretty irresponsible'; Musk replied that Zuckerberg's understanding of the subject was limited.
Zuckerberg and LeCun (Meta's chief AI scientist) both championed open-weight AI as safer and better for innovation; LeCun founded FAIR under Zuckerberg in 2013.
LeCun left Meta after the reorganization around LLM-centric Meta Superintelligence Labs to pursue world-model research, a path he had argued was necessary beyond LLMs.
From 'Open Source AI Is the Path Forward' (July 2024) to being 'careful about what we choose to open source' for superintelligence-class models (July 2025).
Shifted priority from the metaverse (company renamed Meta in 2021) to AI, starting with the 'year of efficiency'.
Both argued the risk of under-investing in AI infrastructure exceeds the risk of over-investing.
Liang argued closed-source moats like OpenAI's are temporary and cannot stop others catching up.
Amodei argued DeepSeek's cost reductions were on the expected efficiency trend rather than a unique breakthrough and that export controls should be maintained.
Released DeepSeek-R1 reasoning model weights under the MIT license.
AlexNet (Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton, 2012) trained on NVIDIA GPUs catalyzed NVIDIA's pivot to deep learning; Huang has cited this moment often. Not re-documented this session.
